subject: 연명 치료를 멈추는 결정
title: When treatment should stop
content: Medicine can now sustain breathing and circulation long after recovery has become impossible. This capacity created a moral question that earlier generations never faced, since the decision to stop is now a decision somebody must make rather than an event that simply arrives. A first distinction concerns withholding and withdrawing. Many people feel that never starting a treatment is easier to justify than removing one already running, and yet careful argument finds no moral difference between them. If a treatment would not be started because it cannot help, then continuing it because it was started is a decision governed by timing rather than by the patient's good. Treating the two differently also creates a perverse incentive, since clinicians reluctant to withdraw become reluctant to try. A second distinction concerns intention. Giving a drug to relieve pain while knowing it may shorten life differs from giving a drug in order to end life, and most legal systems and many moral traditions rest a great deal of weight on that difference. Whether the distinction can bear that weight is genuinely disputed, although the underlying judgment — that using death as a means differs from accepting it as a side effect — has considerable force. The deepest question concerns whose judgment governs. A competent patient's refusal of treatment is decisive, since bodily authority belongs to them, and no benefit to others overrides it. Where the patient cannot decide, the standard shifts to what they would have wanted, and where even that is unknown, to what serves their interests. Each step down that ladder is less reliable than the one above it. What follows in practice is a strong argument for saying beforehand what one wants. The value of an advance directive lies not in its legal force but in relieving a family of a decision they cannot make well while grieving, and that relief is a genuine good.

subject: 마우리아 제국의 바위 비문
title: An ancient king who published his regrets
content: Scattered across the subcontinent, carved on boulders and on polished stone pillars, stand inscriptions issued by a Mauryan emperor in the third century before our era. They are among the earliest datable written records from ancient India, and they are unlike almost anything else surviving from the ancient world. Royal inscriptions of that era ordinarily announce conquests. These do the opposite. In the most famous of them the king describes a campaign he had won, states the numbers killed and deported, and declares that the suffering caused him deep remorse. He then announces that he will pursue his aims through moral persuasion rather than through arms. Whatever his private motives, no other ancient monarch left such a text. The inscriptions carry practical instruction as well. They urge respect between religious communities, kindness to servants and animals, care for the aged, and attention to the claims of every group. Officials are told to tour their districts and hear complaints, and the king declares that he wishes to be informed of business at any hour. Read as history, the texts describe an administrative programme rather than mere piety. Their placement is deliberate. They stand at borders, at pilgrimage sites, and beside trade routes, so the audience was travellers and local populations rather than the court. Several are written in the local script and language of their region, which shows an empire aware that its subjects did not share one tongue. Modern knowledge of them is recent. The script had been unreadable for centuries and was deciphered only in the nineteenth century, after which a king remembered dimly in later legend was recognised as the author of the stones. The civilization he ruled had left its clearest testimony in a form nobody could read for nearly two thousand years.

subject: 유전자 선택과 부모의 권한
title: Choosing what a child will be
content: Techniques now permit some selection among possible children, and further capacity seems likely. The moral arguments provoked by this are unusually confused, partly because several quite different worries get bundled together under a single objection. Separating them makes the discussion tractable. One worry concerns harm to the child. Where a procedure carries physical risk, the case for caution is straightforward and requires no special principle. This worry is genuine but temporary, since it turns on the state of the technique rather than on selection itself. A second worry concerns the relation between parent and child. Parenting has been described as accepting whoever arrives, and selection replaces that acceptance with specification. Critics argue that a child chosen for particular traits enters a relationship shaped by expectations they never agreed to, and that this alters the moral character of family life. The reply notes that parents already shape children enormously through upbringing, so the difference may be of degree rather than kind. A third worry concerns everybody else. If selection becomes common, traits currently regarded as ordinary variation may come to be seen as avoidable defects, and people living with them face a world that treats their existence as an error somebody failed to prevent. This consequence does not depend on any individual choice being wrong, which makes it difficult to address through decisions taken one family at a time. A fourth worry concerns distribution. Where the capacity is purchased, advantages already inherited by the wealthy would be extended into biology, and justice has enough difficulty with the advantages that circulate now. What follows is that a blanket verdict is unavailable. Preventing serious disease and selecting for preferred characteristics raise different questions, and treating them as one issue has made the public argument considerably worse than it needs to be.

subject: 희귀병 치료비의 배분
title: Paying enormous sums for very few people
content: Treatments for rare conditions frequently cost more per patient than any other medicine, sometimes by a factor of hundreds. A health system with a fixed budget must decide whether to fund them, and doing so means that resources are not available elsewhere. The moral argument here is unusually sharp, because both answers have serious costs. The case against funding is a straightforward appeal to numbers. The same money spent on common conditions would produce far more benefit measured in years of life or in suffering avoided, therefore a system aiming at the best outcome overall should decline. Anybody who accepts that health resources are limited has already accepted the logic of this argument, whatever they feel about its conclusion. The case for funding takes several forms. One appeals to the rule of rescue, observing that we treat an identified person in danger differently from a statistical one, and that this response reflects something about moral relations rather than mere sentimentality. A second argues that a system which never funds rare conditions abandons a group entirely, whereas patients with common conditions are helped by many other programmes. Justice may require attention to how burdens fall rather than only to their total. A third consideration concerns why the prices are so high. Where a monopoly sets the figure and the buyer cannot walk away, the cost is a negotiating position rather than a fact of nature, and treating it as fixed concedes the argument before it starts. What the case reveals is that priority setting cannot be reduced to arithmetic. Any defensible answer must state which principles it is applying and accept the consequences openly, and the worst practice is a system that funds by publicity while claiming to decide by evidence.

subject: 잉카의 결승 기록 체계
title: Records tied in knots
content: The Inca empire administered a territory stretching thousands of kilometres, collected tribute, moved populations, and maintained roads and storehouses, all without a writing system of the familiar kind. What it had instead were khipu: bundles of cords, knotted at intervals, hanging from a main cord. Their study is among the more unusual problems in the archaeology of the ancient Americas. A good deal is understood. The knots encode numbers in a decimal arrangement, with position along the cord marking the place value and knot type marking the digit, and cords hanging from other cords express hierarchy. Specialists using these devices could record quantities of grain, cloth, or people, and Spanish accounts from the century of the conquest describe officials reading such records aloud with confidence. What remains disputed is whether they recorded anything besides numbers. Colonial sources mention khipu used to relate histories and genealogies, which would require encoding words rather than quantities. Cord colour, fibre, direction of twist, and spacing all vary in ways that could carry meaning, and several surviving examples resist a purely numerical reading. Nobody has yet demonstrated a decipherment. The difficulty is structural. Roughly a thousand examples survive, most stripped of any record of where they came from or what they concerned, and there is no bilingual key comparable to those that opened other ancient scripts. Colonial authorities destroyed many, regarding them as instruments of an older religion. Recent work has taken a promising direction by matching a small number of khipu against Spanish administrative documents from the same villages, which supplies the context that isolated cords lack. Progress of that kind is slow, and it depends on a civilization's records having been filed twice, once in knots and once by its conquerors.

subject: 백신 접종은 의무인가
title: When protection depends on nearly everyone
content: Some protections work only if most people participate. Where a disease spreads between people, an individual's vaccination protects others as well as themselves, and once enough have taken it the disease cannot circulate at all. This structure generates a moral question that individual choice alone cannot settle. The argument for an obligation runs as follows. The benefit is produced collectively, everybody enjoys it, and somebody who declines while others comply takes the protection without contributing to it. That pattern is unfair regardless of consequences, since the objector relies on exactly the participation they are refusing. Where the personal risk of participating is small and the collective benefit large, the case is strong. The argument against begins with bodily authority. A person's claim to determine what enters their body is among the most firmly held in moral thought, and it is not ordinarily overridden by benefits to others, however large. We do not compel blood donation, and the reasoning that would compel vaccination might compel a great deal else. A second consideration concerns trust, since coercion applied to a suspicious population can harden the suspicion it was meant to overcome. Between compulsion and pure choice lie many arrangements. Requirements attached to particular settings, such as schools or hospitals, restrict less than a general mandate while protecting those most at risk. Making participation easy, free, and convenient raises rates substantially without any coercion at all, and evidence suggests these measures accomplish more than penalties do. What the argument establishes is that a genuine obligation exists while the means of enforcing it remain contested. Recognising the duty without insisting on the harshest instrument is a defensible position, and it is more honest than pretending either that nothing is owed or that anything may be imposed.

subject: 도자기 유약의 우연과 통제
title: The glaze that the fire decides
content: A potter shapes a vessel, applies a coating, and places it in a kiln, and what emerges is not entirely what was intended. Glaze is a layer of glass formed on the surface during firing, and its final colour and texture depend on the composition, the temperature, the atmosphere inside the kiln, and where the piece happened to stand. This art has always involved a partnership with chance. Some traditions worked to reduce that uncertainty. Chinese kilns of the medieval centuries achieved consistency across enormous production, developing recipes and firing schedules that yielded the same result thousands of times, and the resulting wares travelled across the world as luxury goods. Consistency was itself the aesthetic achievement, since a uniform pale green or a flawless white demonstrates control over every variable. Other traditions valued exactly the opposite. Japanese tea ceramics prize surfaces where the ash of the fire settled unevenly, where the glaze pooled and crawled, and where a crack in the coating produced a pattern nobody designed. The potter arranges the conditions and then accepts the outcome, and the resulting object records an event rather than executing a plan. Neither approach is technically simpler. Cultivating accident requires knowing precisely which accidents a given clay and kiln will produce, so the apparent looseness rests on deep familiarity. A potter who cannot control the fire cannot deliberately release control of it. What the two approaches express is a difference in aesthetic value rather than in skill. One tradition finds beauty in the demonstration of mastery, the other in the visible presence of something outside the maker's will. Both understandings persist, and contemporary studio practice draws on each, which is why two pots from the same workshop may be judged by entirely different standards.

subject: 자화상과 화가의 시선
title: The painter looking at themselves
content: A self portrait is made under conditions no other portrait shares. The sitter cannot be posed, since any movement of the head moves the gaze; the artist works from a mirror, so the image is reversed; and the expression recorded is always that of somebody concentrating on painting. These constraints have shaped the tradition in ways worth noticing. The gaze is the most conspicuous. Because the painter looks at the mirror, the finished face looks directly at whoever stands before the picture, which is comparatively rare in other portraiture. Consequently self portraits confront the viewer, and artists have exploited that confrontation deliberately, sometimes softening it by turning the head while the eyes remain fixed. The mirror also explains why so many painters appear to work with the wrong hand. The genre served several purposes at once. It supplied a model who was always available and never charged a fee, which mattered for artists learning to render flesh and expression. It also asserted status, since including the tools of the craft, or dressing as a gentleman rather than a labourer, made a claim about where painting stood among human activities. That claim was contested for centuries. The most interesting examples use the form to examine change. Several artists produced self portraits across decades, and viewing the sequence records ageing more intimately than any other kind of art can, because the same hand and the same attention are applied to the same subject at intervals. What such series display is not merely a face altering but a shifting relation between the painter and their own image. What makes the genre distinctive is that the artist is simultaneously the maker, the model, and the first viewer. No other work in the tradition collapses those roles, and the resulting pictures carry a self consciousness that portraits of other people rarely achieve.

subject: 무용을 기록하는 일의 어려움
title: Writing down a dance
content: Music has a notation that has served for centuries, allowing a work composed in one country to be performed accurately in another long after its composer died. Dance has nothing comparable in general use, and the absence has shaped the art profoundly. Choreography survives mainly in the bodies of dancers who learned it from dancers who learned it from others. The difficulty is not lack of effort. Systems for recording movement have been invented repeatedly since the seventeenth century, some tracking floor patterns, others using symbols placed on a staff to indicate which part of the body moves, in which direction, and for how long. Several are complete enough to reconstruct a work from the page. Yet almost no company uses them routinely, and the reason is instructive. Movement carries more information than any notation captures. Two dancers may execute identical positions in identical time and produce entirely different effects, because weight, tension, breath, and the quality of transition between shapes are what the audience actually reads. A notation recording position and duration preserves the skeleton while losing what the tradition regards as the art. Consequently transmission has remained personal. A dancer who worked with a choreographer carries the work, teaches it to the next generation, and the piece changes slightly with each transmission, exactly as an oral tradition does. Film has helped enormously since the twentieth century, although a recording preserves one performance rather than the work itself, and it flattens the spatial relationships that a viewer in the theatre perceives. What follows is that dance holds an unusual position among the arts. Much of its history before recording is simply gone, known through descriptions and pictures that cannot restore it, and the repertoire that survives does so because particular people took the trouble to remember and to teach.

subject: 사하라 암각화가 남긴 기후 기록
title: Pictures on rock in a desert that was green
content: Across the central Sahara, on cliff faces and in rock shelters, are thousands of engraved and painted images. They show cattle being herded, people swimming, elephants, giraffes, and hippopotamus. All of these belong to a landscape of grass and standing water, and the ancient artists made them in what is now among the driest places on the planet. The pictures are therefore evidence about the past environment as well as about the people who made them. Their sequence records a transformation. The oldest images show wild animals and hunters, a later group shows herds of cattle with their keepers, and the most recent show horses and then camels, which suits an increasingly arid ground. Read alongside sediment cores from ancient lake beds, the sequence matches a known shift: a wet phase lasting several thousand years, ending gradually as the monsoon retreated southward. What the art adds is the human side of that change. A civilization of herders occupied this ground for millennia, and the paintings show their tools, clothing, hairstyles, and social arrangements in detail no other source supplies. Their eventual departure was not sudden, since the images thin out over centuries rather than stopping at a date. Some scholars connect the migration toward the Nile with the origins of the civilization that later rose there. Dating remains the central problem. Rock surfaces cannot be dated directly in the way that buried charcoal can, so ages are argued from style, from superimposition where one image overlies another, and from occasional finds in the shelter floors. Consequently the chronology carries wide margins. What is not in doubt is that a desert crossed today with difficulty once supported a substantial population, and the people who lived there left their record where it could not be ploughed away.

subject: 오염의 책임은 누구에게 있는가
title: Who should pay for the damage already done
content: Environmental damage accumulates over long periods, and by the time it becomes serious those who caused most of it may be dead, dissolved, or living in another country. Assigning responsibility therefore involves moral questions that ordinary accounts of wrongdoing handle badly. Several principles compete. The first holds that whoever caused the damage should repair it. This is intuitive and matches how we treat harm generally, although it faces a hard objection where the causing occurred before anybody understood the consequences. Blaming somebody for effects nobody could have foreseen conflicts with the principle that responsibility requires the possibility of knowing. A second principle assigns the cost to whoever benefited. Even where the original actors were blameless, their descendants and successors inherited wealth built on the activity, and holding an unearned benefit derived from a harm creates a claim upon the holder. This avoids the knowledge objection entirely, since it rests on the benefit rather than on fault. A third principle looks to capacity, assigning the burden to whoever can most easily bear it. This appeals to a widely shared judgment about how collective costs should fall, although it disconnects the duty from the damage altogether, which strikes many as arbitrary. Each principle produces a different distribution, and disputes about environmental obligation are frequently disputes about which one applies without either side saying so. Progress in such arguments usually comes from noticing that the principles overlap in most real cases, since those who caused the damage, those who benefited, and those who can pay are frequently the same parties. Where they diverge, honesty requires stating which principle is being invoked and why. What cannot be defended is the position that because responsibility is complicated, nobody bears any, since the damage is real and somebody will bear its consequences whether or not anybody accepts the duty.

subject: 인형극의 손과 목소리
title: Giving life to something obviously not alive
content: Puppet theatre asks an audience to attend to an object while knowing it is an object. The strings are visible, the operator may stand in plain sight, and nobody is deceived. Yet audiences respond to a well handled puppet as though it had intentions, and understanding why reveals something about how any theatrical art works. The response depends on movement rather than on likeness. A puppet with a crudely carved face will seem alive if its weight shifts before it walks, if it looks at what it is about to touch, and if it breathes. Puppeteers speak of these as the fundamental disciplines, and audiences detect their absence immediately even when they could not name what was missing. Consequently the art lies in the timing of attention rather than in the carving. Traditions differ enormously in what they hide. Some conceal the operator entirely behind a screen, using shadow or a raised booth, so the figure appears autonomous. Others place the handlers in full view dressed in black, and the audience learns within minutes to stop seeing them. The Japanese tradition goes further by dressing the principal operator in ceremonial clothing and lighting him fully, so the relation between manipulator and figure becomes part of the performance. Voice is handled with equal variety. In some cultures the puppeteer speaks; in others a separate chanter delivers every character while musicians accompany, which separates the voice from the movement and requires the two performers to breathe together. What the whole art demonstrates is that theatrical belief does not require illusion. Spectators are not tricked and do not forget what they are watching, and yet they attend to the figure as an agent. The same double awareness operates whenever an audience weeps at an actor they know is acting, and puppetry simply makes the mechanism visible.

subject: 정형시 형식의 제약과 자유
title: Why poets accept rules they could ignore
content: A fixed poetic form specifies how many lines a poem has, how long each line runs, and where the rhymes fall. Poets working in such forms accept restrictions that nothing compels them to accept, and readers unfamiliar with the tradition frequently regard the practice as arbitrary decoration. The defence offered by poets themselves is more interesting. The first claim is that constraint generates invention. A writer who may say anything in any manner faces too many options and tends toward the first phrasing that arrives. A writer who needs a particular rhyme in a particular position must search, and the search turns up connections that would not have occurred otherwise. Consequently the form functions as a machine for producing surprise, and many poets report that their best lines were found rather than intended. The second claim concerns shape. A fixed form carries expectations about where the argument turns, and readers who know the tradition feel the turn arrive. A sonnet that shifts direction at the expected place satisfies, and one that delays the shift creates tension precisely because the delay is measurable against the convention. None of that is available to a poem with no shape to depart from. The third claim concerns memory. Metre and rhyme make lines hold in the mind, which mattered enormously before printing and still shapes what people can carry with them. Cultures without writing developed elaborate formal traditions for exactly this reason, and their forms are more demanding rather than less. What the practice finally demonstrates is that freedom in art is not the absence of constraint. A poet choosing a form chooses which difficulties to face, and the resulting work is made partly of the resistance encountered, which is why free verse when it succeeds imposes its own equally strict demands.

subject: 탄소 배출권 거래의 윤리
title: Whether pollution may be bought and sold
content: Systems that cap total emissions and allow the resulting permits to be traded are defended as efficient, since reductions occur wherever they are cheapest. The moral objections raised against them are frequently dismissed as economically naive, and yet several deserve a hearing on their own terms. The first objection holds that trading permits transforms a wrong into a price. Where somebody may pay to continue polluting, the payment functions as a fee rather than a penalty, and the moral stigma that might have changed behaviour is removed. Evidence from other domains supports the mechanism: introducing a fine for a behaviour sometimes increases it, because participants conclude that the matter has been settled financially. A second objection concerns where reductions occur. Efficiency implies that emissions fall wherever it is cheapest, which frequently means far from those who produced them, and local pollutants accompanying carbon emissions therefore stay concentrated in the same communities. Justice attends to distribution as well as to totals, and a system indifferent to location will reproduce existing inequality. The defence is substantial. A cap sets an absolute limit that trading does not raise, so the environmental outcome is determined by the cap rather than by the market. Trading merely allocates the reductions, and doing so cheaply means a tighter cap becomes politically achievable. On this reading the moral objections apply to weak caps rather than to trading itself. What the argument suggests is that the design carries the moral weight. A generous cap with free permits distributed to existing polluters rewards them for past emissions; a tight cap with permits auctioned and revenue returned looks quite different. Debating the instrument in the abstract has produced a great deal of argument and very little agreement, while the details that actually matter receive far less attention than they deserve.

subject: 아동문학에서 그림과 글의 분업
title: When the pictures say something the words do not
content: A picture book is not an illustrated story. In the strongest examples the words and the images carry different information, and the meaning emerges from the space between them, which makes the form more sophisticated than its audience might suggest. Consider the simplest case of divergence. The text may report that nothing unusual happened while the pictures show a disaster unfolding behind the speaker, so a child who can look but not yet read perceives the joke immediately. This arrangement gives the young reader an advantage over the narrator, and the pleasure of that advantage is one of the tradition's characteristic effects. A second use of the division concerns emotion. Words in this art form tend toward restraint, and the pictures supply what the text withholds. A story about loss may state only what was done while the images record the feeling, which allows a reader to approach a difficult subject at whatever pace they choose. Adults reading aloud frequently notice that the child is studying the picture long after the sentence has ended. The design constraints are severe. A picture book runs to a fixed number of pages determined by how paper folds, the turn of the page is a dramatic instrument, and the text must be short enough to be read many times without exhausting the adult reading it. Working within these limits is closer to writing verse than to writing prose. Consequently the form has attracted serious artists throughout its history, and the best examples reward attention that their apparent simplicity conceals. A culture that treats such work as a minor branch of literature misjudges it, since teaching somebody to read images against words is among the more useful things any art can do.

subject: 포스터 미술과 대중 설득
title: Art designed to be seen at a distance
content: The poster emerged as an art form in the late nineteenth century, when printing allowed large sheets in strong colour to be produced cheaply. Its conditions of viewing were unlike those of any earlier picture: seen from across a street, competing with other posters, and holding a passer-by for perhaps two seconds. Everything about the aesthetic follows from those conditions. Detail is useless at that distance, so the tradition developed flat areas of colour, heavy outlines, and shapes readable as silhouettes. Text and image had to be designed together rather than one added to the other, which brought lettering into the composition as a formal element. Artists working in the medium learned to build a picture around a single idea, because a poster that requires interpretation has already failed. The form served commerce first and then politics. Wartime governments discovered its power quickly, and the propaganda campaigns of the twentieth century produced some of the most technically accomplished work in the tradition, along with the most troubling. A design that persuades effectively persuades regardless of whether the message deserves it, which is why the history of this art cannot be separated from arguments about manipulation. Its influence spread widely. Painters borrowed the flattened space and bold outline, and the visual language of the poster shaped how the twentieth century looked at everything from packaging to film titles. Several of the artists regarded as major figures in modern art worked in the medium without regarding it as lesser. What the form demonstrates is that severe practical constraints can generate a distinctive aesthetic rather than merely limiting one. The poster had to work in two seconds at thirty metres, and meeting that requirement produced a visual tradition that outlasted the products it was made to sell.

subject: 아바스 시대의 번역 운동
title: The century that moved a library between languages
content: Beginning in the eighth century, scholars working under the Abbasid caliphs took on one of the largest translation efforts in history. Greek works on medicine, star lore, number, and thought were put into Arabic, along with texts from Persian and Sanskrit, and the work went on for roughly two hundred years. What came of it reached far beyond the region where it took place. The movement was paid for on purpose. Caliphs, officials, and rich families sent agents to hunt for books, sometimes in distant lands, and hired teams to render them. Because the tongues were unrelated, the task called for more than swapping words: a whole set of terms had to be coined, and Arabic gained a language for science that it had not held before. Teams often made several drafts of one text, fixing each as they came to grasp it better. These scholars did not merely pass things on. Working through the ancient books exposed errors, gaps, and clashes, and the notes written beside the translations often put them right. Star tables were worked out again against fresh watching, medical accounts were tried against practice, and methods in number were pushed further. So the century of translation was also a century of new work, and telling the two apart is often impossible. What happened next is well known. From the twelfth century, scholars in Spain and Sicily turned many of these Arabic books into Latin, and much ancient learning reached medieval Europe by that road rather than straight from the Greek. Several works live only in the Arabic. What the episode shows is how knowledge really moves between one civilization and another. It needs money, schools, and steady care across lifetimes, and it happens where a people decide that books written by foreigners in a dead tongue are worth the cost.

subject: 사진이 회화에서 가져간 일
title: What painting stopped having to do
content: When photography became practical in the middle of the nineteenth century, painters faced a machine that could record appearances faster, cheaper, and more accurately than any hand. Predictions that the older art would die were common and turned out to be wrong, although the relationship between the two reshaped painting profoundly. The most obvious effect was the loss of a function. Portraits of ordinary people, records of places, and documentation of events had supported a great many painters, and that work moved rapidly to the camera. What remained was whatever painting could do that photography could not, and the search for that territory occupied much of the following century. Several answers emerged. Colour was one, since early photographs were monochrome and painters could pursue chromatic effects unavailable to the camera. Another was the visible mark, because a photograph conceals its making while a brushstroke declares it, and traditions emphasising the surface of the picture made a virtue of exactly that difference. A third was subjectivity: a painting could record how something felt to a particular observer rather than how it appeared to a lens. Influence ran the other way as well. Photographs of figures in motion revealed that horses gallop differently from how painters had always shown them, and artists adjusted. The camera's arbitrary cropping, cutting figures at the frame edge, appeared in painting shortly afterwards, since the accident of the snapshot suggested a compositional freedom the older tradition had not used. What the episode illustrates is how a new medium alters an existing art rather than replacing it. Painting became more interested in what painting is, which is a question artists had not needed to ask while their work was chiefly a service. The aesthetic developments that followed were made possible by a machine that took the job away.

subject: 자동화가 없앤 일자리에 대한 책임
title: What is owed to those whose work was replaced
content: Machines have displaced human labour repeatedly, and the historical record suggests that employment eventually recovers in new forms. This observation is frequently offered as a complete answer, and it is not one, because the people displaced in any particular episode are rarely the people who fill the new positions. The moral question concerns them rather than the aggregate. Consider what the displaced person loses. Income is the obvious part, although evidence from regions where an industry collapsed suggests that the damage extends considerably further, into health, family stability, and the standing of a whole community. Skills built over decades become worthless, and the value of that loss does not appear in any calculation showing that total output rose. The case for an obligation rests on how the gains and losses are distributed. Automation produces a surplus, and that surplus flows to owners, to consumers through lower prices, and to workers in expanding sectors. The costs fall almost entirely on a small group who happened to hold the replaced positions. Where a change makes society better off in total while devastating an identifiable minority, justice supplies a familiar answer: those who gain should compensate those who lose, and the transaction is still worth making afterwards. The objection is that nobody promised anybody a permanent job, and that protecting existing work would freeze progress. This has force against preserving positions and none whatever against compensating people. The distinction matters enormously, since the two responses have entirely different effects on whether the change happens at all. What follows is that the argument about automation has been conducted in the wrong terms. Whether the displacement should occur and what is owed to those displaced are separate questions, and answering the first affirmatively does nothing to answer the second.

subject: 애니메이션의 프레임과 착시
title: Movement built out of stillness
content: Animation produces motion from a sequence of still images, and every choice about how those images are made and timed becomes an artistic decision. Understanding the underlying mechanism explains why the tradition developed the particular aesthetic it did. The eye does not simply blur successive pictures together. What the viewer supplies is an inference that the object in the second image is the same object seen slightly later, and that inference operates over a surprisingly wide range. Consequently animators discovered that images need not be numerous or accurate to read as movement; they need to be placed so that the inference is easy. Many traditions draw new pictures only every second or third frame without any loss of smoothness. This discovery produced a set of principles that animators still teach. Exaggerating a movement before it begins, stretching a form as it accelerates, and letting parts of a figure lag behind the main mass all depart from how bodies actually behave, and yet they read as more convincing than accurate depiction does. The reason is that the viewer is inferring rather than observing, and the inference responds to emphasis. Different cultures made different bargains with the cost of drawing. Studios in one tradition invested in full animation with fluid motion throughout, while others developed a style holding a single drawing while the background moves or the camera pushes in, concentrating effort on a few striking images. That constraint became an aesthetic, and the resulting visual language is now valued for its own qualities rather than excused as economy. What the art demonstrates is that a medium's limitations shape its beauty. Nothing about a sequence of drawings requires the exaggerated timing that animation developed, and yet the tradition arrived there because the viewer's inference rewards it, which makes this an art built directly on a fact about perception.

subject: 영화 음악이 관객을 이끄는 법
title: The score you are not supposed to notice
content: Music in film performs a great deal of work while remaining largely beneath attention. Audiences leaving a cinema rarely describe the score, and yet their experience of nearly every scene was shaped by it. Examining how the tradition operates reveals techniques that are quite specific and largely invisible. The most basic function is telling the audience how to feel about what they see. An identical shot of a person walking down a corridor becomes threatening, comic, or melancholy depending entirely on what accompanies it, and viewers experience the resulting emotion as coming from the image. This is why composers speak of the score as an argument about the scene rather than an accompaniment to it. A second function concerns continuity. Film assembles fragments shot at different times, and music running across a cut binds them into a single passage, smoothing transitions that would otherwise register as interruptions. Sequences covering long spans of time depend almost entirely on this, since the music supplies the connection that the images lack. A third function is anticipation. A score can signal that something is about to happen several seconds before it does, which builds tension, or it can withhold that signal so that an event arrives unprepared. Composers describe the placement of these cues as the most demanding part of the work, because a warning arriving too early dissipates and one arriving too late has no effect. The tradition has also developed the deliberate absence of music. Silence in a film where the audience has been trained to expect a score becomes conspicuous, and directors use it for exactly that reason. What the art demonstrates is that an aesthetic instrument can be most effective when the audience does not know it is being used.

subject: 전시 동선의 설계
title: The route a museum builds for you
content: A visitor entering a gallery believes they are choosing where to walk. In practice the route has been designed, and the design carries an argument about what the objects mean and in what order they should be understood. Exhibition planning is among the less visible arts, and its decisions shape the experience more than most visitors realise. The simplest choice is between a forced sequence and an open floor. A corridor arrangement guarantees that everybody encounters the material in the intended order, which suits a story that builds, and it is frequently used for historical narratives. An open plan lets visitors wander, which suits collections where comparison matters more than sequence, although it risks leaving the argument unmade. Most galleries combine the two, using sightlines rather than walls to suggest a path. Sightlines do a great deal of the work. Placing a striking object where it is visible from the entrance draws people toward it, and everything they pass on the way is seen in relation to that destination. Designers speak of anchors and of rest points, since attention degrades after a certain number of objects and a room with fewer works allows recovery. The number of pieces shown is therefore a decision about attention rather than about available space. Labels complete the design. Their length determines how long somebody stands still, which determines how many people the room can hold, and their content determines what is noticed in the object beside them. A label mentioning a detail causes visitors to look for it; one that does not leaves the detail invisible. What follows is that a museum presents an interpretation whether or not it intends to. Choosing not to guide is itself a choice, and the resulting experience will be shaped by whatever the architecture happens to emphasise.

subject: 송대 도시의 야간 시장
title: When a capital stopped closing at dusk
content: Chinese cities of the earlier medieval centuries were organised into walled wards whose gates closed at nightfall. Movement after dark required official permission, and commerce occupied designated enclosures that shut with everything else. During the Song era this arrangement broke down, and what replaced it changed urban life across the empire. Shops spread along the streets rather than remaining inside assigned enclosures, the ward walls became irrelevant, and the curfew was abandoned in the major cities. A famous scroll painted in the twelfth century shows the resulting scene: a river crowded with boats, a bridge lined with stalls, and streets busy with people, animals, and goods. Written accounts from the same era describe districts where food was sold through the night. The change followed population growth and a shift in how the ancient administrative model was applied. Cities had grown beyond what the ward system could contain, and enforcement had become impractical long before it was abandoned. Consequently the reform ratified a situation rather than creating one, which is a common pattern in the history of regulation. Contemporary writers left detailed descriptions of what could be bought and at what hour, and their catalogues of dishes, entertainments, and specialist trades are among the richest sources for daily life anywhere in the medieval world. They record storytellers, puppet performances, and shadow plays continuing past midnight, along with the establishments that fed the audiences. Historians disagree about how far the change extended beyond a few great cities. What is clear is that the civilization of this era developed an urban culture with no obvious parallel elsewhere at the time, and that its collapse before invasion from the north was remembered afterwards with the particular grief reserved for a way of life that could be described precisely.

subject: 자율 무기와 책임의 공백
title: When a machine selects the target
content: Weapons that identify and engage targets without a person deciding each case raise a moral problem that older technology did not. Every previous instrument left a human being at the point of decision, so responsibility could be traced to somebody who chose. Removing that person creates a gap that existing frameworks were not built to close. Consider who might bear responsibility for a wrongful killing by such a system. The commander who deployed it did not select the target and may not have been able to predict the selection. The programmer wrote general rules rather than deciding any particular case. The manufacturer supplied a product working as specified. Each participant can truthfully say that the outcome was not their decision, and yet somebody died. Some argue that the gap is illusory, since deploying a system whose behaviour cannot be predicted is itself a decision for which the commander answers fully. This response has force, although it requires holding somebody responsible for an outcome they could not foresee, which conflicts with the principle that responsibility tracks control. A second argument holds that machines may eventually discriminate more reliably than people under combat stress, so refusing them could cost civilian lives. That claim is empirical and currently unproven, and the response to it is that the moral standing of the decision matters independently of accuracy. Being killed by a process that no person chose to apply to you differs from being killed by somebody who decided, even where the outcomes match. What the debate reveals is that our moral vocabulary for war depends heavily on the presence of a deciding agent. Rules about proportionality, discrimination, and surrender all address somebody making judgments, and a technology that removes the judge leaves the rules without anyone to obey them.
